lead: In a balanced three-phase circuit, every phase carries the same current magnitude and the same phase angle. The supply gives two sets of numbers: line values at the terminals and phase values inside each winding or load branch. They differ by √3, but the total power follows one formula, P = √3 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ, whether the load is star or delta. This lets a 400 V motor, a factory feeder and a distribution transformer be rated from a few terminal measurements.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.6 for star and delta connections and Chapter 2.5 for active, reactive and apparent power.

sections.h3: Star connection: line voltage is √3 times phase voltage

blocks.text: Line voltage V<sub>L</sub> is measured between any two line terminals. Phase voltage V<sub>ph</sub> is measured across one phase winding or one load branch; in star it is the voltage from one line to the neutral point. Line current I<sub>L</sub> flows in a line conductor. Phase current I<sub>ph</sub> flows inside one phase branch. Voltages are in volts (V) and currents in amperes (A).
In a star connection, the three phase branches meet at the neutral point. Each line feeds exactly one branch, so the line current is the branch current: I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>.

Take two phase voltages from the neutral to two lines. They have equal magnitude and are 120° apart. Their difference is the line voltage between those two lines. The resultant magnitude is 2V<sub>ph</sub>cos 30° = √3 V<sub>ph</sub>. The line voltage also leads the corresponding phase voltage (neutral to line) by 30°; in delta, the line current lags the corresponding phase current by 30°.

blocks.where: V<sub>L</sub> is line voltage in V; V<sub>ph</sub> is phase voltage in V; I<sub>L</sub> is line current in A; I<sub>ph</sub> is phase current in A. Some syllabi write V<sub>LL</sub> for V<sub>L</sub>.

blocks.text: For a 400 V line, V<sub>ph</sub> = 400/√3 = 231 V. This is the usual single-phase level in a 400 V three-phase distribution system.

sections.h3: Delta connection: line current is √3 times phase current

blocks.text: In a delta connection, each phase branch is connected between two lines. There is no neutral point. The voltage across a branch is therefore a line voltage: V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>.

The line current is not the branch current. At a line terminal, two branch currents meet. By Kirchhoff's current law, the line current is their vector difference. The two phase currents have equal magnitude and are 120° apart. Their difference has magnitude 2I<sub>ph</sub>cos 30° = √3 I<sub>ph</sub>.

blocks.where: V<sub>L</sub> is line voltage in V; V<sub>ph</sub> is phase voltage in V; I<sub>L</sub> is line current in A; I<sub>ph</sub> is phase current in A.

blocks.text: The √3 factor moves in opposite ways in the two connections. Star gives a larger line voltage and the same current. Delta gives the same voltage and a larger line current. Both statements assume a balanced load: equal phase impedances and equal phase angles.

sections.h3: Total active, reactive and apparent power

blocks.text: For one phase, active power is V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ. Here φ is the angle by which the phase current lags or leads the phase voltage in that branch. For three identical phases, total active power is three times the per-phase value.

blocks.where: P is active power in watts (W); φ is the angle between phase voltage and phase current; cos φ is the power factor; V<sub>ph</sub> and I<sub>ph</sub> are phase voltage and phase current; V<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> are line voltage and line current.

blocks.text: For a star load, substitute V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3 and I<sub>ph</sub> = I<sub>L</sub>: 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub> = 3(V<sub>L</sub>/√3)I<sub>L</sub> = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>. For a delta load, substitute V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>ph</sub> = I<sub>L</sub>/√3: 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub> = 3V<sub>L</sub>(I<sub>L</sub>/√3) = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>. The line formula is the same for both.

blocks.where: Q is reactive power in volt-amperes reactive (var); S is apparent power in volt-amperes (VA); φ is the same phase angle between phase voltage and phase current; V<sub>L</sub> and I<sub>L</sub> are line voltage and line current.

blocks.text: The power factor is cos φ = P/S. Use line values in the √3 formulas and phase values in the 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub> formula. Mixing the two sets is the most common calculation error.

figure.caption: In the delta example, the 400 V line voltage is also the phase voltage; phase current then sets line current by √3, and line quantities give active and apparent power.

examples.question: A balanced delta load has phase impedance 15∠45° Ω and line voltage 400 V. Find the phase current, line current, active power and apparent power.
steps: For a delta load, phase voltage equals line voltage: V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> = 400 V.
The phase impedance magnitude is 15 Ω and its angle is 45°. Phase current magnitude: I<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>/|Z| = 400/15 = 26.67 A.
In delta, line current: I<sub>L</sub> = √3 I<sub>ph</sub> = 1.732 × 26.67 = 46.19 A.
Power factor: cos φ = cos 45° = 0.7071. Active power: P = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ = 3 × 400 × 26.67 × 0.7071 = 22,627 W = 22.6 kW.
Check with line values: P = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ = 1.732 × 400 × 46.19 × 0.7071 = 22.6 kW.
Apparent power: S = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub> = 3 × 400 × 26.67 = 32,000 VA = 32.0 kVA. Or S = √3 × 400 × 46.19 = 32.0 kVA.
examples.answer: The phase current is 26.67 A, the line current is 46.19 A, the active power is 22.6 kW and the apparent power is 32.0 kVA.
examples.check:
import math
VL = 400.0
Z = 15.0
phi = math.radians(45.0)
Vph = VL
Iph = Vph / Z
IL = math.sqrt(3.0) * Iph
P = 3.0 * Vph * Iph * math.cos(phi)
S = 3.0 * Vph * Iph
print(f'{Iph:.2f}')
print(f'{IL:.2f}')
print(f'{P/1000:.1f}')
print(f'{S/1000:.1f}')

traps: Do not put line current into P = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ. That formula uses phase voltage and phase current only.

In the √3 formula, φ is the phase angle of the load, the angle between phase voltage and phase current. In a balanced circuit the angle between line voltage and line current is the same φ, so either measurement gives the same power factor. Only with an unbalanced load does each phase have its own angle.
In star, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3, not V<sub>L</sub>. In delta, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>, not V<sub>L</sub>/√3.
Do not mix V<sub>ph</sub> with I<sub>L</sub> in one formula. Use either all phase quantities with the factor 3, or all line quantities with the factor √3.
The √3 relations and total-power formulas here assume a balanced load. For an unbalanced load, solve each phase separately or use another method.

quiz.q: Define line voltage and phase voltage for a star-connected balanced load.
quiz.a: Line voltage V<sub>L</sub> is the voltage between any two line terminals. Phase voltage V<sub>ph</sub> is the voltage across one phase branch, from one line to the neutral point in star.

quiz.q: Why does √3 appear in the star relation V<sub>L</sub> = √3V<sub>ph</sub>?
quiz.a: Two phase voltages from neutral to two lines are equal in magnitude and 120° apart. The line voltage is their vector difference. Its magnitude is 2V<sub>ph</sub>cos 30°, which equals √3V<sub>ph</sub>.

quiz.q: A balanced star load has line voltage 400 V, line current 10 A and power factor 0.8 lagging. Find active power.
A balanced delta load has 20 Ω per phase and line voltage 400 V at unity power factor. Find phase current, line current and active power.
A student writes P = 3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ for a star load. What is wrong?
quiz.a: The factor 3 belongs with phase quantities: P = 3V<sub>ph</sub>I<sub>ph</sub>cos φ. For line quantities the factor is √3: P = √3V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos φ. Using 3 with line values overstates power by √3.

quiz.q: The same balanced load is reconnected from star to delta at the same line voltage.Compare phase voltage, phase current and total power.
quiz.a: In star, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>/√3. In delta, V<sub>ph</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>, so phase voltage becomes √3 times larger. Phase current also becomes √3 times larger. Total power becomes 3 times larger, because power depends on phase voltage times phase current for three phases.

quiz.q: In a balanced delta load, why is the line current larger than the phase current?
quiz.a: Each line terminal carries the vector difference of two phase-branch currents. These two currents are equal in magnitude and 120° apart, so their difference has magnitude √3 times the phase current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power engineers use per-unit line and phase quantities to compare transformers and feeders of different voltage levels. Sequence components extend the same ideas to unbalanced faults and protection settings. Motor nameplates combine line voltage, line current and power factor into the same √3 power formula. Search for per-unit system, symmetrical components and three-phase power measurement to go further.
